chapter:
Expressions
Overview
Expressions are the core computational units of Scaly. Every expression evaluates to a value; one that answers nothing answers the empty tuple (). An expression is an operation: a sequence of things — values, names, operator names, tuples, vector literals and blocks — that the compiler reads from left to right. It holds one current value, and the type of that value says what the next thing means:
current value next thing meaning
none, a prefix, or one waiting for its operand an operator name a prefix: it takes the next value (-x, a - -2, not not a)
a value an operator its type declares that operator; it waits for its right operand
a function a tuple the call; the tuple is the argument list
a function one other value the call with that one argument (print "hi", twice -5)
a type a tuple the construction (Point(1, 2))
a type a vector literal the generic instance (Vector[int])
a value a vector literal indexing (v[i])
any as T, is T the cast or the test of the whole operation so far
Parentheses make a tuple (and a tuple of one value is that value, so they also group), brackets a vector literal, braces a block, and the dot a member. Nothing else structures a sequence: there is no precedence table in the compiler. How strongly operators bind is stated by the standard library, as a protocol of pending types: a + answers a value that waits for its right operand, and the protocol decides what an operator after it means. The levels, strongest first, are listed under .
Two consequences are worth knowing before reading the rest of this chapter:
Application is stronger than waiting. Before an operator takes what follows, that thing takes what is applied to it: a + f(1) adds the call's result, a + v[i] the element.
A call without parentheses takes exactly one thing. print f(x) is (print f)(x), which the compiler reports; an argument that is itself a call, an indexing or a construction takes its parentheses: print(f(x)).
